The federal statistical system—one of the pillars of how we understand this country—has faced extraordinary pressure. Programs have been halted. Funding has been threatened or withdrawn. Statistical leaders have been dismissed. Institutions designed to operate independently have faced increasing political pressure. Many of us have lost our jobs or found our work threatened. The American Statistical Association reported that all 13 federal statistical agencies lost staff in 2025, with some, like the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)—at least temporarily—almost totally demolished (American Statistical Association 2025). The shuttering of USAID halted critical research projects and is projected to lead to a staggering number of avoidable deaths (Cavalcanti et al. 2025). These systems were built over decades. The people who have dedicated their lives to these objectives have created a body of knowledge that is essential to understanding the way we live and how that changes—the statisticians and survey methodologists, analysts and researchers, project managers and directors, contractors and subcontractors. There has been messaging through DOGE actions and other high-level communications that the work of these individuals is biased, wasteful, unneeded, or worse. Many of those people are members of this community. And this rhetoric and these actions are having a profound effect. One experienced federal researcher told me she was considering getting out of the field altogether. She couldn’t see a path forward for herself. We are losing some of our greatest assets and future leaders. For those that remain, we bear witness to their integrity, persistence, and quiet professionalism as they continue to produce evidence when the environment around them is uncertain and unsupportive. We see and empathize with the “survivors’ guilt” many experience. We also recognize the disruption in the lives of many who have lost their positions and now face remaking their careers. They must do so at a time when uncertainty and trepidation have affected the entire industry, making it a less-than-hospitable place for job seekers and career changers. A displaced federal worker I spoke to said she feels a sense of grief and loss. Grieving not only for her own personal losses, but for the bigger picture of what is happening to federal government data collection, to public health research, and to the scientific community. I spoke to a small business owner who saw critical work that she and her colleagues had done shelved, to possibly never see the light of day. A graduate student shared with me the challenges she has experienced—having her research funding terminated, seeing fewer placements for her fellow students at universities, and being forced to grapple with new worries about her international student status. She said, “When I was coming to the US, I didn’t think that I would have to worry that scientific research could be compromised in a country like this.” Others shared: “The last 18 months have felt like a ticking countdown clock”; “The institutional knowledge we have lost will take years to recover”; and “The foundation is shakier than I thought.” I want to acknowledge the extreme stress that has characterized our field and so many of our members in 2025 and 2026 and bear witness to the professional and personal toll this has taken. Next, I want to talk about the importance of our work. At its core, what we do is deceptively simple. We ask people about their lives—how they live, think, work, and experience the world. We do so carefully, systematically, and with the goal of understanding more than just the loudest voices. The importance of that work becomes clearer in moments like this, when increasingly, we are living in a world where the idea of shared evidence itself is contested. Where data can be dismissed because it is inconvenient. Where research can be labeled fraudulent if it challenges power. Some specific examples of this are the lawsuits against Ann Selzer (Doyle 2024); the litigation threats to the New York Times (Svirnovskiy 2026), CNN (Grynbaum and Haberman 2020), and their research partners; the demand for cancellation of programs deemed focused on DEI (Exec. Order No. 14151 2025; Hsu 2025); and the removal of nonbinary gender categories from federal research (Exec. Order No. 14168 2025), to name just a few. This runs counter to everything our field stands for. We may never measure perfectly. But through rigorous methods and transparency, we highlight the experiences, hopes, and fears of everyday Americans. In a democracy, that matters. Because governing without understanding the public is governing in the dark. What we produce is not just data. It is a record. A record of what people think, what they experience, and how society is changing. We must protect that, celebrate it, and feel pride in the importance of the work that we do. A researcher at the Census told me that she was most proud to be part of a system where, despite current narratives, the goal is to “measure truth, to the best of our ability, across time, across administrations, and across events.” Through all of this, the work continues. A statistician at a large research company spoke of his pride in what we do. He said, “Linking what people are thinking and saying to policy has never been more important.” I now want to reflect on the community, because this work does not happen in isolation. It depends on a diverse and interdependent community. The work we do is the product of government, academia, nonprofit organizations, and the private sector. Each plays a distinct role. Government statisticians establish benchmarks. Academics develop and test new ideas and train future researchers. Nonprofit and election researchers help us understand civic life. And commercial researchers innovate—finding ways to make data collection more scalable and accessible. We often approach problems differently. We use different methods. We operate under different constraints. We do not always agree (looking at you, AAPORnet). We debate probability and nonprobability sampling (boy, do we debate probability and nonprobability sampling!). We debate qualitative and quantitative approaches. We debate new tools, new data sources, and, more recently, artificial intelligence. These debates can be intense. They can feel divisive. But they exist because we are all trying to answer the same questions: How do we understand people accurately? How do we do this work responsibly? And how do we do it within real-world budgetary and time constraints? Our disagreements are a sign of a healthy scientific community—a community that makes our work possible, improves it, and, at times, helps us bear it. Multiple people I spoke to talked about the importance of having people to turn to that believe in the work that we do, to bounce ideas off of, to call when we need questions answered. A sympathetic human to talk to, not an obsequious chatbot. The government employees I spoke to remarked on how important this community has been in making it possible to keep going when they felt disparaged, and in helping make connections in the search for a new opportunity. A private-sector researcher reflected on how we share expertise to improve the work for us all, even when there could be commercial reasons for not doing so. A multicultural researcher noted that perhaps our recent struggles have brought us together. She said, “I have co-pollinated with so many others that I wouldn’t have before, because we’re working through the same struggles.” A methodologist at a start-up company noted that through all this craziness, he is seeing more acceptance and creativity in our community; more openness to the wide variety of practices and innovations. I can see frustration among our ranks as we debate how to respond to today’s challenges, how to move forward, how to value and publicize what we do. Some have called for the community to have a stronger voice. Some have expressed that doing so would put their membership at risk. Some have suggested our separating ourselves based on method. Some have felt marginalized, seeing the work that they do categorized as lesser. I urge our community to recognize that what unites us is more important than our differences. Remember that your fellow researchers are seeking to do just what you are doing—increase our understanding of a given population or issue. They may be doing it with different methods, budgets, and styles, but we are united in seeking clarity, and we are family in this enterprise. Be kind to each other. Seek to understand and empathize. Show respect for your fellow researcher, even if the work that they do seems only marginally connected in our big Venn diagram of the research industry (see figure 1). Humorous Venn diagram depicting our shared commitment to research. Now, what do we do with all of this? How will we respond to this moment—not just endure it, but build a more resilient, innovative, and inclusive future for our field? This is why AAPOR is so important. Through AAPOR we can support the work and strengthen the community that makes it possible. AAPOR facilitates the critical work of public opinion research by creating task forces, providing forums for debate and discussion, educating on best practices, and evolving standards for the industry. Our work on cell phone samples and text messaging has paved the way for the wide use of new methodological tools. Our pre-election polling task forces have changed the way we conduct and talk about election research. Our reports on opt-in and probability panels have given us frameworks for transparency and a shared language for these sample sources, to name just a few examples. Our response to these times should be to keep driving forward. We must continue what AAPOR has done for 81 years—help the industry understand itself, improve what we do, and identify new challenges and opportunities. In the past 18 months, through these challenging times, AAPOR has released major resources on pre-election polling (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025a), establishment surveys (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025b), texting for research (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025c), linking survey and nonsurvey data (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025d), and, most recently, on responsible AI integration (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2026). We have updated our code of professional ethics and practices, hosted webinars and short courses, organized new workshops, and put together two major conferences. Table 1 highlights a small selection of these achievements. Selected AAPOR resources and activities produced during 2025–2026. All of this is carried out by volunteers, supported by a small staff, who work collaboratively, from their different vantage points and experiences, to express the latest information about our field. Keeping this collaborative enterprise going is what will keep our industry vibrant and resilient through these times, and it is what AAPOR does best. AAPOR’s response is also to foster the community doing this important work. We are A Meeting Place (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2020). Every year, through our conference, we provide an opportunity to come together to share ideas and network. If lately the conference has felt like a therapy session (as in figure 2), it is needed for us to support each other during these times. Cartoon highlighting AAPOR’s annual conference as a place for mutual support around the emergence of AI. Created by author using ChatGPT. We also need to ensure that our industry is expanding and inclusive. AAPOR’s commitment to diversity has helped reshape the field and made this organization stronger and better able to respond to today’s challenges. We must continue to prioritize this. The AAPOR Affinity Groups give us more ways to connect and share our challenges. As shown in table 2, today we have 11 Affinity Groups, including ConsultPOR, formed in early 2026 in part as a reaction to the movement of practitioners out of traditional employee settings into business for themselves, and the Global Research Affinity Group, inaugurated at our May 2026 Conference. List of AAPOR Affinity Groups as of May 2026. We need to provide tangible, practical support to our community as well. Last year, when so many faced layoffs, travel restrictions, and financial hardships, we rallied as a community and raised a record amount of donations to support conference travel grants. We also provide upskilling sessions, professional development, job coaching, and networking opportunities, all led by volunteers in this room and beyond. In terms of our individual responses, the people I spoke with offered a clear message: steady on, stay curious, and do this together. One academic said, “We need to keep doing what we have always been doing—learning, innovating, and using evidence-based approaches.” A business owner urged us to “lean into the unknown.” And a student reminded me that when we multiply our efforts with others, “it’s way stronger than we can imagine.” My call to action today reflects these sentiments. Stay the course, seek help when you need it, and provide a hand up to another when you can. And don’t give up. Because what we do is important. The industry has faced challenges before: shifts in methodology, new technologies, declining response rates, new forms of data, and now a double whammy of a federal administration hostile to research and the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence. What do we do? We engage with these challenges. We communicate our values. We set standards. We adapt our practices. And we continue the work. Get involved. AAPOR needs each of you. Join a committee. Say “yes” if I ask you to run for council! Ask me, or any of us on council, how to participate. Be a deeper part of this organization that provides a voice, a space, and a framework for what we do. Get involved outside of AAPOR, too. Write local op-eds, contact your representatives, reach out to colleagues in need, and support causes that support the industry, including AAPOR. Join us in this moment, in this community, and in being the way forward. As I close, I want to return to where I began. How do we bear witness to the moment we are living through? And how do we ensure that this work and this community can thrive in the years to come? AAPOR has existed for more than eight decades. Through profound change, the purpose of this work has remained remarkably consistent: to create valid and transparent data about behaviors, attitudes, and characteristics that enable informed societal decision-making. That work is not always easy. But it remains essential. Because no society can understand itself without evidence about the people who live within it. When we do this work well—carefully, ethically, and openly—we create something larger than a dataset, report, or publication. We create a record of the public’s voice. In that sense, this field helps our society bear witness to itself. One of the people I talked to said, “We are writing history right now.” How we respond to this moment is something future researchers will examine. They will seek to understand the foundations of our systems that produce evidence. They will ask how those systems were challenged. And they will ask what we did in response. Our responsibility is to strengthen what we do, improve our tools, defend our standards, and support one another. We continue by doing what this field has always done: help the public be heard, help society understand itself, and strengthen the democracy that depends on both.

Jordon Peugh: Chief Business Officer, SSRS , Glen Mills, PA,

items.summary_ko: AAPOR 회장은 2025~2026년 연방 통계·과학 제도의 압박과 공공의견 연구 공동체가 겪은 고용·연구 환경의 불안정을 증언하고, 증거 기반 민주주의에서 조사 연구의 중요성을 강조한다. 연설은 AAPOR의 표준·교육·토론·상호지원 기능과 연구자들의 협력·참여를 통해 연구의 질과 공동체의 회복력·포용성을 지켜야 한다고 제안한다.
items.title: AAPOR Presidential Address AAPOR Presidential Address 2026: Bearing Witness to This Moment

items.abstract: We present the first causal evidence that female politicians are more likely to face political violence. Using fourteen years of data on attacks against Italian politicians, we show that marginally elected female mayors—similar to men and elected in comparable towns—are three times as likely to be attacked. We find no gender differences in policy platforms, policymaking, performance, or corruption. Instead, violence emerges independently on women's choices, consistently with discrimination - rather than political influence - driving the gap in violence. Female mayors are less likely to seek re-election after attacks, highlighting violence’s role in perpetuating the gender gap.
items.summary_ko: 이탈리아 정치인에 대한 14년간의 공격 자료를 활용해, 유사한 지역에서 근소한 차이로 당선된 여성 시장이 남성 시장보다 공격을 받을 확률이 약 세 배 높은지 분석했다. 정책 성향·정책 결정·성과·부패에는 성별 차이가 없었으며, 공격 격차는 정치적 영향력보다 차별과 일치했고 공격받은 여성 시장은 재출마 가능성이 낮았다.
items.title: Attacking Women or their Policies? Understanding Violence against Women in Politics

items.abstract: Ensuring that student leaders uphold integrity and ethical standards is a key concern for future governance and public administration, as many eventually assume leadership roles in both public and private sectors. Employing the Reasoned Action Approach, this study examined student leaders’ understanding of corruption and integrity, the factors that hinder them from upholding integrity, and the factors that shape their perceptions of corruption and integrity. Data were gathered through key informant interviews with student leaders. The findings revealed that weak accountability systems, pressure from peers, political party influence, and uninspiring leadership traits exhibited by national leaders were major barriers to upholding integrity, ultimately undermining ethical leadership. The study further found that student leaders’ perceptions of corruption are shaped by personal beliefs, social expectations, and institutional experiences. The findings highlight the need for improved governance structures, ethical mentorship, and training programmes to cultivate future leaders with strong moral foundations.

Justice Nyigmah Bawole: King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals

items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 합리적 행위 접근법을 활용해 가나 대학 학생 지도자들의 부패·청렴 인식과 청렴 실천을 저해하거나 형성하는 요인을 주요 정보제공자 인터뷰로 분석했다. 약한 책임성 체계, 또래 압력, 정당의 영향, 국가 지도자들의 고무적이지 않은 리더십이 청렴 실천의 주요 장벽으로 나타났으며, 개인적 신념·사회적 기대·제도적 경험이 부패와 청렴에 대한 인식을 형성했다.
items.title: Youth and Corruption in Ghana: Perspectives from University Student Leaders
Elite Interactions and Social Bonds: How Partisan Cooperation Shapes Perceptions of Cross-Party Friendships

items.abstract: Persistent inequalities in political knowledge are a central concern in political communication. We organize the mechanisms underlying the knowledge-gap literature by distinguishing between individual preconditions, structural features of the information environment, and topic characteristics. Within this framework, we note that self-directed information seeking, a prototypical form of intentional exposure, has received little attention despite its importance in navigating today’s complex information environment. We conducted a field experiment in Germany, combining randomized encouragements and passive browser tracking, to examine how individuals with varying education levels acquire policy-specific knowledge through online search. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions (verbal encouragement, financial encouragement, or control) to seek information on three salient policy topics differing in divisiveness and complexity (child support, energy transition, and cannabis legalization). We estimated both intention-to-treat (ITT) and local average treatment effects (LATE) of information seeking on post-search knowledge outcomes, with a focus on education and civic knowledge as moderators. While the interventions equalized information-seeking behavior, the results provide some support for the knowledge gap hypothesis: knowledge gains were concentrated among participants with higher education or baseline civic knowledge, who, according to our post-hoc exploratory analyses, appeared more effective at navigating search results. These findings indicate that a narrowing of knowledge inequalities goes beyond motivation: it calls for both individual-level interventions to strengthen citizens’ skills and structural-level adaptations to foster more equitable learning environments.
items.summary_ko: 온라인 검색을 통한 정책 정보 습득에서 교육수준에 따른 지식 격차가 줄어드는지를, 독일 참가자를 대상으로 한 무작위 현장실험과 브라우저 추적으로 분석했다. 정보탐색 행동은 개입으로 균등해졌지만, 지식 증가는 고학력자나 기초 시민지식이 높은 참여자에게 집중되어 지식 격차 가설을 일부 지지했다.
items.title: The Knowledge Gap in a High-Choice Media Environment: Experimental Evidence from Online Search

items.abstract: Abstract When political elites and activists promote anti‐discrimination policies, they often frame discrimination as violating liberal moral values such as fairness, care for vulnerable groups, and equality. However, this approach may fail to resonate with conservative voters and could even alienate them. Through two separate studies, this article uses a multi‐method approach to examine the moral values held by supporters and opponents of discrimination and test how conservative and liberal value appeals influence acceptance. The findings reveal that values like loyalty, care for the in‐group, authority, and sanctity appear in acceptors' justifications and that framing discrimination as a violation of these values, associated with conservatism, reduces acceptance across the political spectrum. Contrastingly, appealing to values associated with liberalism backfires and increases Republicans' acceptance. While liberal values were central in shifting social norms towards anti‐discrimination, appealing to conservative values may be more effective in reducing contemporary acceptance of discrimination.

Ida Bruun Nørregaard: Geschwister‐Scholl‐Institute of Political Science, LMU Munich Germany
Department of Political Science Aarhus University Aarhus C Denmark

items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 차별 지지자와 반대자의 도덕적 가치와, 보수·진보적 가치 호소가 인종·민족 차별 수용에 미치는 영향을 두 개의 다방법 연구로 검토했다. 내집단 충성·돌봄, 권위, 신성성에 호소하면 정치 성향과 관계없이 차별 수용이 감소했으며, 진보적 가치 호소는 공화당 지지자의 수용을 오히려 높였다.
items.title: How moral values underpin and affect attitudes on ethnic discrimination

items.abstract: Abstract Existing scholarship on propaganda in authoritarian regimes centers on whether it persuades or coerces. Within the persuasion camp, researchers have examined how factors such as message source, content, credibility, and audience demographics shape propaganda effectiveness. This study shifts attention to psychological needs. Drawing on evidence from China, it integrates multi‐round survey experiments, a virtual lab‐in‐the‐field experiment using a mobile news app developed by the author, text analysis of state media, and field interviews. The results show that propaganda appealing to the need to belong, the need to maintain self‐esteem, or the need to express core values is most effective among individuals for whom the corresponding need is particularly strong—but generalized propaganda, even when psychologically engaging, is not. The findings suggest that propaganda is most persuasive when targeted to stable psychological orientations rather than designed for broad consumption. These findings have implications for understanding how authoritarian regimes sustain public support: propaganda effectiveness depends not only on content or reach, but also on how closely its psychological appeals correspond to the stable motivational orientations of its audience. The shift in authoritarian communication strategies toward psychologically targeted appeals makes the mechanisms identified here increasingly relevant to understanding contemporary propaganda.

Xiaoxiao Shen: Department of Political Science Northeastern University Boston Massachusetts USA

items.summary_ko: 권위주의 체제의 선전이 어떤 심리적 욕구와의 부합을 통해 설득력을 얻는지 중국 사례로 분석했다. 다중 라운드 설문실험, 모바일 뉴스 앱을 활용한 현장 실험, 국가 매체 텍스트 분석, 현장 인터뷰를 종합한 결과, 소속감·자존감 유지·핵심 가치 표현 욕구에 호소하는 선전은 해당 욕구가 강한 사람에게 가장 효과적이지만, 심리적으로 매력적이더라도 일반화된 선전은 그렇지 않았다.
items.title: When propaganda resonates

items.abstract: Abstract The ontological security of states may be threatened by the politics of empathy. Empathy—as a contested affective‐political field—has a capacity to both consolidate and unravel dominant understandings of identity, security, political subjectivity, and self‐other relations. This article connects a politics of empathy to patterns of state violence and resistance in situations of conflict and authoritarian politics, arguing that the distribution of feeling that underpins a politics of empathy is structured by positionality, power, and social context. The article argues that states construct “affective regimes” through which they seek to manage the legitimate subjects of empathy in order to maintain their ontological security, and focuses on empirical testimony from the Syrian uprising in 2011 and the Assad regime's strategies of violence to explore these affective dynamics. It reveals ways in which the state's efforts are always resisted and transgressed by citizens, generating counter‐narratives of security‐identity and affective relations. A politics of empathy offers analytical tools for understanding the construction and effectiveness of states' affective regimes to maintain ontological security as well as being normatively essential to the task of challenging forms of state power, political violence, and generating alternative imaginings of ontological security and subjectivity.

Naomi Head: School of Social and Political Sciences University of Glasgow Glasgow UK

items.summary_ko: 공감의 정치가 국가의 존재론적 안보를 어떻게 강화하거나 위협하는지 분석하고, 국가는 공감의 정당한 대상을 관리하는 ‘감정 체제’를 구축하지만 시민들의 저항과 일탈로 이에 대한 대항적 안보·정체성 서사가 생성된다고 주장한다. 2011년 시리아 봉기의 경험적 증언과 아사드 정권의 폭력 전략을 바탕으로, 이러한 감정 역학과 국가 권력·정치적 폭력에 도전하는 공감의 가능성을 탐구한다.
items.title: Affective regimes and ontological security: When empathy threatens the state

items.abstract: Abstract Social dominance orientation (SDO) refers to how much a person generally opposes group‐based equality and supports group‐based dominance. SDO is measured as an individual difference and pertains very broadly to people's socio‐political attitudes and perceptions, to endorsement or rejection of political parties and candidates, and to behaviors that enforce organizational hierarchies. This paper reviews empirical evidence published from 2010 to 2024 concerning social dominance orientation, first presenting evidence of its stability over time and measurement integrity, next showing that, across numerous cultures and languages and ways of measuring group prejudice and stereotypes, SDO correlates with prejudice favoring people in dominant groups rather than people in subordinate groups, and that this effect is stronger within dominant groups than subordinate groups. Similarly, we review evidence that people higher on SDO are more anti‐social and tend to take hierarchy‐enhancing rather than hierarchy‐attenuating roles. We then delve into the psychology of SDO and summarize the evidence for the relation of SDO and closed cognitive styles, low scores on humility‐honesty, and low concern for other people rather than the self. Using existing adult and child development studies, we outline two processes by which higher SDO may develop: one based on learning to categorize and to rank categories as superior/inferior, and one based on parents' emphasis on obtaining high status to gain approval. We conclude by outlining the next questions that might be pursued.

Felicia Pratto: Department of Psychological Sciences University of Connecticut Storrs CT USA

items.summary_ko: 이 논문은 2010~2024년의 경험적 연구를 검토해 사회적 지배지향성(SDO)의 안정성과 측정 타당성, 집단 간 편견·고정관념 및 위계 강화 행동과의 관계, 그리고 SDO의 발달 경로를 종합한다. 검토 결과, SDO가 높은 사람일수록 지배집단을 선호하는 편견과 반사회적·위계 강화 성향이 강했으며, 이러한 성향은 범주화·서열화 학습과 부모의 높은 지위 강조를 통해 발달할 수 있는 것으로 나타났다.
items.title: Social dominance orientation

items.abstract: ABSTRACT A central challenge in government contracting is fostering cooperation between buyers and sellers where contract terms are incomplete. This article introduces a framework for formal‐relational contracting (FRC) in public sector contexts, where rigid regulations, competing values, and market imperfections make cooperation both difficult and valuable. FRC promotes cooperation through contract terms defining shared goals, guiding principles, and governance mechanisms. We present the theoretical foundations of FRC and examine its potential through 320 government contract management decision simulations where public contract managers acted as government buyers and business sellers facing sequential choices under both FRC contracts and the more conventional formal contracting approach. The results show that FRC increased managers' cooperative behavior by around 30 percentage points compared to formal contracting. Qualitative evidence further suggests that FRC shifted managers' mindsets from adversarial to cooperative. We discuss theoretical and practical implications for how FRC can enhance cooperation and mutual value in government contracting.

Lena Brogaard: Department of Social Sciences and Business, Centre for Research on Public‐Private Collaboration Roskilde University Roskilde Denmark
Matthew Potoski: Bren School of Environmental Science and Management University of California – Santa Barbara Santa Barbara California USA
Ole Helby Petersen: Department of Social Sciences and Business, Centre for Research on Public‐Private Collaboration Roskilde University Roskilde Denmark

items.summary_ko: 불완전한 계약조건에서 정부 구매자와 판매자의 협력을 높일 수 있는지 검토하기 위해, 공공 계약관리자 320명이 순차적 선택을 수행하는 의사결정 시뮬레이션에서 공식-관계적 계약(FRC)과 전통적 공식 계약을 비교했다. FRC는 공식 계약보다 협력적 행동을 약 30%포인트 높였으며, 관리자들의 사고방식도 대립적 태도에서 협력적 태도로 전환한 것으로 나타났다.
items.title: Improving Cooperation in Government Purchasing Through Formal‐Relational Contracting

items.abstract: Smart city initiatives, as public service innovation, represent a major evolution within state-led meta-governance, requiring complex inter-participant collaboration. Yet scholarship often treats these networks as static, missing how governance structures adapt to digital uncertainties. To fill this gap, this study employs stochastic actor-oriented models and collaborative governance theory to examine the evolution of network structures and participant attributes across 3482 smart city projects in China. Results reveal three governance patterns: government-dominated, government-SOE hybrid, and multi-stakeholder. Transitive triads, age similarity, geographic proximity, and size heterogeneity promote evolution, while outdegree constrains it. Findings guide optimizing partner selection and strengthening adaptive governance.
items.summary_ko: 이 연구는 중국의 스마트시티 프로젝트 3,482건을 대상으로 디지털 불확실성 속 협력적 거버넌스 네트워크와 참여자 속성이 어떻게 진화하는지 분석했다. 확률적 행위자 지향 모형과 협력적 거버넌스 이론을 적용한 결과, 정부 주도형·정부-공기업 혼합형·다중 이해관계자형의 세 패턴이 나타났으며, 전이적 삼각관계·연령 유사성·지리적 근접성·규모 이질성은 네트워크 진화를 촉진하고 외향 연결 정도는 이를 제약했다.
items.title: Navigating the digital transformation: unravelling the dynamic evolution of smart city collaborative governance networks

items.abstract: Experiments on how cognitive biases, such as social and historical reference points and negativity bias, shape citizens’ evaluations of government performance have produced mixed findings, which typically come from Western contexts and focus on single reference points. To address these gaps, we replicated (N = 3710) and extended (N = 2356) Olsen’s ‘Compared to what?’ to interactions between multiple social and historical reference points in Hong Kong. Very low baselines are found in the replication alongside trivial evidence for the importance of reference points in citizens’ performance evaluations and negativity bias. In the extension, we found that (1) when both social and historical reference points are presented to participants, they have stronger effects when negative information is provided and (2) the effects of combinations of historical and social reference points differ across policy domains. Though survey experiments can be noisy, the study demonstrates the value of replication to question the generalization of cognitive biases.

Jiasheng Zhang: The Chinese University of Hong Kong

items.title: Reference points, negativity bias and citizens’ performance evaluations: a replication and extension

items.abstract: When I first became AAPOR’s vice president/president-elect in 2024, I thought I might focus my presidential address on something like “the business of research,” reflecting my perspective as chief business officer of a research company and considering how the association might think about its financial stability and growth. Then in 2025, a little something happened… A new administration arrived and took a chainsaw to the statistical and scientific institutions of this country. A national leader sued and threatened some of the most public faces of our industry. And the economic fallout of these and other actions shook our industry to the core. Once I got out of the fetal position, I had to grapple with new priorities for my AAPOR presidency. So today, what I want to do is bear witness to this time we are living through and provide hope for the future. There are four things I will reflect on: the moment we are in; the work we do; the community that makes that work possible; and how we respond to these times. I want to present not just my own voice, but those across our community. To do so, I have talked to members from a wide variety of fields, experiences, and circumstances. I share their views, along with my own, and I thank them for the honesty, vulnerability, and inspiration they gave me. We are living through a period of profound instability in the systems that produce and protect evidence. The federal statistical system—one of the pillars of how we understand this country—has faced extraordinary pressure. Programs have been halted. Funding has been threatened or withdrawn. Statistical leaders have been dismissed. Institutions designed to operate independently have faced increasing political pressure. Many of us have lost our jobs or found our work threatened. The American Statistical Association reported that all 13 federal statistical agencies lost staff in 2025, with some, like the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES)—at least temporarily—almost totally demolished (American Statistical Association 2025). The shuttering of USAID halted critical research projects and is projected to lead to a staggering number of avoidable deaths (Cavalcanti et al. 2025). These systems were built over decades. The people who have dedicated their lives to these objectives have created a body of knowledge that is essential to understanding the way we live and how that changes—the statisticians and survey methodologists, analysts and researchers, project managers and directors, contractors and subcontractors. There has been messaging through DOGE actions and other high-level communications that the work of these individuals is biased, wasteful, unneeded, or worse. Many of those people are members of this community. And this rhetoric and these actions are having a profound effect. One experienced federal researcher told me she was considering getting out of the field altogether. She couldn’t see a path forward for herself. We are losing some of our greatest assets and future leaders. For those that remain, we bear witness to their integrity, persistence, and quiet professionalism as they continue to produce evidence when the environment around them is uncertain and unsupportive. We see and empathize with the “survivors’ guilt” many experience. We also recognize the disruption in the lives of many who have lost their positions and now face remaking their careers. They must do so at a time when uncertainty and trepidation have affected the entire industry, making it a less-than-hospitable place for job seekers and career changers. A displaced federal worker I spoke to said she feels a sense of grief and loss. Grieving not only for her own personal losses, but for the bigger picture of what is happening to federal government data collection, to public health research, and to the scientific community. I spoke to a small business owner who saw critical work that she and her colleagues had done shelved, to possibly never see the light of day. A graduate student shared with me the challenges she has experienced—having her research funding terminated, seeing fewer placements for her fellow students at universities, and being forced to grapple with new worries about her international student status. She said, “When I was coming to the US, I didn’t think that I would have to worry that scientific research could be compromised in a country like this.” Others shared: “The last 18 months have felt like a ticking countdown clock”; “The institutional knowledge we have lost will take years to recover”; and “The foundation is shakier than I thought.” I want to acknowledge the extreme stress that has characterized our field and so many of our members in 2025 and 2026 and bear witness to the professional and personal toll this has taken. Next, I want to talk about the importance of our work. At its core, what we do is deceptively simple. We ask people about their lives—how they live, think, work, and experience the world. We do so carefully, systematically, and with the goal of understanding more than just the loudest voices. The importance of that work becomes clearer in moments like this, when increasingly, we are living in a world where the idea of shared evidence itself is contested. Where data can be dismissed because it is inconvenient. Where research can be labeled fraudulent if it challenges power. Some specific examples of this are the lawsuits against Ann Selzer (Doyle 2024); the litigation threats to the New York Times (Svirnovskiy 2026), CNN (Grynbaum and Haberman 2020), and their research partners; the demand for cancellation of programs deemed focused on DEI (Exec. Order No. 14151 2025; Hsu 2025); and the removal of nonbinary gender categories from federal research (Exec. Order No. 14168 2025), to name just a few. This runs counter to everything our field stands for. We may never measure perfectly. But through rigorous methods and transparency, we highlight the experiences, hopes, and fears of everyday Americans. In a democracy, that matters. Because governing without understanding the public is governing in the dark. What we produce is not just data. It is a record. A record of what people think, what they experience, and how society is changing. We must protect that, celebrate it, and feel pride in the importance of the work that we do. A researcher at the Census told me that she was most proud to be part of a system where, despite current narratives, the goal is to “measure truth, to the best of our ability, across time, across administrations, and across events.” Through all of this, the work continues. A statistician at a large research company spoke of his pride in what we do. He said, “Linking what people are thinking and saying to policy has never been more important.” I now want to reflect on the community, because this work does not happen in isolation. It depends on a diverse and interdependent community. The work we do is the product of government, academia, nonprofit organizations, and the private sector. Each plays a distinct role. Government statisticians establish benchmarks. Academics develop and test new ideas and train future researchers. Nonprofit and election researchers help us understand civic life. And commercial researchers innovate—finding ways to make data collection more scalable and accessible. We often approach problems differently. We use different methods. We operate under different constraints. We do not always agree (looking at you, AAPORnet). We debate probability and nonprobability sampling (boy, do we debate probability and nonprobability sampling!). We debate qualitative and quantitative approaches. We debate new tools, new data sources, and, more recently, artificial intelligence. These debates can be intense. They can feel divisive. But they exist because we are all trying to answer the same questions: How do we understand people accurately? How do we do this work responsibly? And how do we do it within real-world budgetary and time constraints? Our disagreements are a sign of a healthy scientific community—a community that makes our work possible, improves it, and, at times, helps us bear it. Multiple people I spoke to talked about the importance of having people to turn to that believe in the work that we do, to bounce ideas off of, to call when we need questions answered. A sympathetic human to talk to, not an obsequious chatbot. The government employees I spoke to remarked on how important this community has been in making it possible to keep going when they felt disparaged, and in helping make connections in the search for a new opportunity. A private-sector researcher reflected on how we share expertise to improve the work for us all, even when there could be commercial reasons for not doing so. A multicultural researcher noted that perhaps our recent struggles have brought us together. She said, “I have co-pollinated with so many others that I wouldn’t have before, because we’re working through the same struggles.” A methodologist at a start-up company noted that through all this craziness, he is seeing more acceptance and creativity in our community; more openness to the wide variety of practices and innovations. I can see frustration among our ranks as we debate how to respond to today’s challenges, how to move forward, how to value and publicize what we do. Some have called for the community to have a stronger voice. Some have expressed that doing so would put their membership at risk. Some have suggested our separating ourselves based on method. Some have felt marginalized, seeing the work that they do categorized as lesser. I urge our community to recognize that what unites us is more important than our differences. Remember that your fellow researchers are seeking to do just what you are doing—increase our understanding of a given population or issue. They may be doing it with different methods, budgets, and styles, but we are united in seeking clarity, and we are family in this enterprise. Be kind to each other. Seek to understand and empathize. Show respect for your fellow researcher, even if the work that they do seems only marginally connected in our big Venn diagram of the research industry (see figure 1). Humorous Venn diagram depicting our shared commitment to research. Now, what do we do with all of this? How will we respond to this moment—not just endure it, but build a more resilient, innovative, and inclusive future for our field? This is why AAPOR is so important. Through AAPOR we can support the work and strengthen the community that makes it possible. AAPOR facilitates the critical work of public opinion research by creating task forces, providing forums for debate and discussion, educating on best practices, and evolving standards for the industry. Our work on cell phone samples and text messaging has paved the way for the wide use of new methodological tools. Our pre-election polling task forces have changed the way we conduct and talk about election research. Our reports on opt-in and probability panels have given us frameworks for transparency and a shared language for these sample sources, to name just a few examples. Our response to these times should be to keep driving forward. We must continue what AAPOR has done for 81 years—help the industry understand itself, improve what we do, and identify new challenges and opportunities. In the past 18 months, through these challenging times, AAPOR has released major resources on pre-election polling (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025a), establishment surveys (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025b), texting for research (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025c), linking survey and nonsurvey data (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2025d), and, most recently, on responsible AI integration (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2026). We have updated our code of professional ethics and practices, hosted webinars and short courses, organized new workshops, and put together two major conferences. Table 1 highlights a small selection of these achievements. Selected AAPOR resources and activities produced during 2025–2026. All of this is carried out by volunteers, supported by a small staff, who work collaboratively, from their different vantage points and experiences, to express the latest information about our field. Keeping this collaborative enterprise going is what will keep our industry vibrant and resilient through these times, and it is what AAPOR does best. AAPOR’s response is also to foster the community doing this important work. We are A Meeting Place (American Association for Public Opinion Research 2020). Every year, through our conference, we provide an opportunity to come together to share ideas and network. If lately the conference has felt like a therapy session (as in figure 2), it is needed for us to support each other during these times. Cartoon highlighting AAPOR’s annual conference as a place for mutual support around the emergence of AI. Created by author using ChatGPT. We also need to ensure that our industry is expanding and inclusive. AAPOR’s commitment to diversity has helped reshape the field and made this organization stronger and better able to respond to today’s challenges. We must continue to prioritize this. The AAPOR Affinity Groups give us more ways to connect and share our challenges. As shown in table 2, today we have 11 Affinity Groups, including ConsultPOR, formed in early 2026 in part as a reaction to the movement of practitioners out of traditional employee settings into business for themselves, and the Global Research Affinity Group, inaugurated at our May 2026 Conference. List of AAPOR Affinity Groups as of May 2026. We need to provide tangible, practical support to our community as well. Last year, when so many faced layoffs, travel restrictions, and financial hardships, we rallied as a community and raised a record amount of donations to support conference travel grants. We also provide upskilling sessions, professional development, job coaching, and networking opportunities, all led by volunteers in this room and beyond. In terms of our individual responses, the people I spoke with offered a clear message: steady on, stay curious, and do this together. One academic said, “We need to keep doing what we have always been doing—learning, innovating, and using evidence-based approaches.” A business owner urged us to “lean into the unknown.” And a student reminded me that when we multiply our efforts with others, “it’s way stronger than we can imagine.” My call to action today reflects these sentiments. Stay the course, seek help when you need it, and provide a hand up to another when you can. And don’t give up. Because what we do is important. The industry has faced challenges before: shifts in methodology, new technologies, declining response rates, new forms of data, and now a double whammy of a federal administration hostile to research and the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence. What do we do? We engage with these challenges. We communicate our values. We set standards. We adapt our practices. And we continue the work. Get involved. AAPOR needs each of you. Join a committee. Say “yes” if I ask you to run for council! Ask me, or any of us on council, how to participate. Be a deeper part of this organization that provides a voice, a space, and a framework for what we do. Get involved outside of AAPOR, too. Write local op-eds, contact your representatives, reach out to colleagues in need, and support causes that support the industry, including AAPOR. Join us in this moment, in this community, and in being the way forward. As I close, I want to return to where I began. How do we bear witness to the moment we are living through? And how do we ensure that this work and this community can thrive in the years to come? AAPOR has existed for more than eight decades. Through profound change, the purpose of this work has remained remarkably consistent: to create valid and transparent data about behaviors, attitudes, and characteristics that enable informed societal decision-making. That work is not always easy. But it remains essential. Because no society can understand itself without evidence about the people who live within it. When we do this work well—carefully, ethically, and openly—we create something larger than a dataset, report, or publication. We create a record of the public’s voice. In that sense, this field helps our society bear witness to itself. One of the people I talked to said, “We are writing history right now.” How we respond to this moment is something future researchers will examine. They will seek to understand the foundations of our systems that produce evidence. They will ask how those systems were challenged. And they will ask what we did in response. Our responsibility is to strengthen what we do, improve our tools, defend our standards, and support one another. We continue by doing what this field has always done: help the public be heard, help society understand itself, and strengthen the democracy that depends on both.

Jordon Peugh: Chief Business Officer, SSRS , Glen Mills, PA,

items.abstract: We present the first causal evidence that female politicians are more likely to face political violence. Using fourteen years of data on attacks against Italian politicians, we show that marginally elected female mayors—similar to men and elected in comparable towns—are three times as likely to be attacked. We find no gender differences in policy platforms, policymaking, performance, or corruption. Instead, violence emerges independently on women's choices, consistently with discrimination - rather than political influence - driving the gap in violence. Female mayors are less likely to seek re-election after attacks, highlighting violence’s role in perpetuating the gender gap.
items.summary_ko: 이탈리아 정치인에 대한 14년간의 공격 자료를 활용해, 유사한 지역에서 근소한 차이로 당선된 여성 시장이 남성 시장보다 공격을 받을 확률이 약 세 배 높은지 분석했다. 정책 성향·정책 결정·성과·부패에는 성별 차이가 없었으며, 공격 격차는 정치적 영향력보다 차별과 일치했고 공격받은 여성 시장은 재출마 가능성이 낮았다.
items.title: Attacking Women or their Policies? Understanding Violence against Women in Politics

items.abstract: Abstract Do sunk costs shape how voters judge political leaders, or do reputational signals carried by current choices dominate? Across three preregistered experiments (total N = 1462) using vignettes about a national rail project, we orthogonally manipulated sunk costs (high vs. absent), leaders' decisions (continue vs. abandon), campaign commitments (pro, anti, none), and reminders of prior voting behavior. In Experiment 1 ( N = 346), Bayesian ANOVA showed that evaluations (vote likelihood, perceived honesty, competence) were reliably higher when leaders continued rather than abandoned a project, with no main effect of sunk costs and no interaction. Experiment 2 ( N = 719) replicated the null sunk‐cost effect and further found no effect of campaign commitments once the leader's current decision was known. Experiment 3 ( N = 397) used a structural equation model to test mediation: perceived commitment—but not perceived sunk costs—robustly predicted evaluations, and abandonment sharply reduced perceived commitment; prior‐vote cues were weak and did not mediate effects. Together, the studies indicate that people take continuation to signal commitment and view it positively, whereas abandonment stopping signals a breach of commitment and is penalized. Apparent sunk‐cost sensitivity in politics may often reflect a premium on consistency rather than waste aversion. We discuss implications for designing “face‐saving” off‐ramps and reframing evidence‐based reversals as fidelity to higher order commitments.

John Michael: Cognition in Action Lab, Department of Philosophy University of Milan Milan Italy
Marco Mattei: Cognition in Action Lab, Department of Philosophy University of Milan Milan Italy

items.summary_ko: 세 차례 사전등록 실험(N=1,462)에서 정치 지도자에 대한 유권자 평가가 매몰비용보다 사업 지속·중단 결정, 선거 공약, 과거 투표 단서에 어떻게 반응하는지 분석했다. 사업 지속은 헌신의 신호로 긍정적으로 평가된 반면 중단은 헌신 위반으로 평가를 낮췄으며, 매몰비용 효과와 공약·과거 투표의 독립적 영향은 지지되지 않았다.
items.title: Consistency, not waste aversion, explains apparent sunk‐cost effects in politics

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial Intelligence (AI) is adopted in public organizations as a transformative innovation, yet how value prioritizations unfold in AI adoption processes remains underexplored. Therefore, we ask: How do public values unfold in AI adoption processes in public organizations? We conducted a qualitative case study of an AI adoption process at the radiology department of a Dutch academic hospital after the decision to adopt is made and before implementation, using ethnographic fieldwork, interviews, and document analysis. Our findings highlight how public values and the AI adoption process are balanced in the transition from the initiation to the implementation stage. We find a recursive relationship between public values and the AI adoption process. We show an interplay of instrumental and intrinsic values. We highlight the importance of top‐down adoption decisions for how public values are perceived, and we show the importance of public organizations ensuring public values are safeguarded in public‐private partnerships.

Bram Klievink: Faculty of Governance and Global Affairs Leiden University Leiden the Netherlands
Jinke M. Oostvogel: Faculty of Governance and Global Affairs Leiden University Leiden the Netherlands
Matthew M. Young: Faculty of Governance and Global Affairs Leiden University Leiden the Netherlands

items.summary_ko: 네덜란드 대학병원 영상의학과에서 채택 결정 이후 구현 이전의 AI 도입 과정을 민족지적 현장연구, 인터뷰, 문서분석으로 분석해 공공가치가 도입 과정과 재귀적으로 상호작용하며, 도구적 가치와 내재적 가치가 조정된다는 점을 밝혔다. 또한 하향식 도입 결정과 민관협력에서 공공가치의 인식 및 보호가 중요함을 제시했다.
items.title: Getting the Priorities Straight: Public Values in AI Adoption

items.abstract: ABSTRACT Public service co‐production is often framed as a means of creating public value, yet its dynamics are complex when citizen‐led participation is catalyzed by strong public institutions. This mixed‐methods study examines government‐catalyzed, citizen‐centric co‐production in Shanghai, China, where the state provides institutional support, policy legitimacy, and infrastructure while citizens undertake much of the work of deliberation, coordination, and implementation. Drawing on 246 interviews and survey data from 1476 residents involved in community new infrastructure projects, we examine how citizen trust, public‐service‐oriented motivation, and perceived co‐production efficacy are associated with process and outcome value creation, and how perceived institutional settings condition these relationships. The findings show that citizen cognitive factors are positively associated with value creation, while stronger perceived institutional settings can negatively moderate these relationships. Recursive qualitative analysis suggests two mechanisms that help interpret this pattern: formal rigidity may crowd out citizen agency in the co‐production process, while informal social density may generate lock‐in effects that weaken the translation of trust into substantive outcomes. The study contributes to co‐production and institutional theory by specifying the boundary conditions under which institutional support becomes over‐institutionalization. Effective co‐production requires not less government, but strong enabling support at the initiation stage combined with greater local discretion, participatory rule revision, and flexible enforcement.

Bing Ran: School of Public Affairs Penn State Harrisburg Middletown Pennsylvania USA
Huanming Wang: School of Public Administration and Policy Dalian University of Technology Dalian Liaoning Province China
Xiaoyun Sun: Department of Public Administration Shandong University of Science and Technology Qingdao Shandong Province China

items.summary_ko: 상하이의 정부 촉진 시민 중심 공동생산에서 시민의 신뢰, 공공서비스 지향 동기, 공동생산 효능감이 가치 창출과 어떤 관련이 있으며 제도적 환경이 이를 어떻게 조건화하는지, 246건의 인터뷰와 1,476명 주민 설문을 활용한 혼합방법으로 분석했다. 시민의 인지적 요인은 가치 창출과 긍정적으로 관련되지만, 경직된 공식 제도와 과도한 제도화는 시민 주체성을 제약하고 사회적 밀도는 신뢰가 실질적 성과로 이어지는 것을 약화시킬 수 있다고 밝혔다.
items.title: The Bureaucratic Paradox of Citizen Agency: Institutional Crowding‐Out in Government‐Catalyzed Co‐Production in Shanghai, China
